course.title: Pandas Mastery
course.subtitle: Complete Data Analysis Program
course.tagline: Learn Data. Understand Data. Analyse Data. Think like a Data Analyst.
course.description: Pandas from the first Series to groupby, merges, time series and a machine-learning hand-off. Twenty modules, ten learning sections each, every code sample executed before it ships, and examples that use BroCode's own data shapes: courses, lessons, quiz attempts and progress.
prerequisites: An idea of what a table is — rows and columns
outcomes: Create, inspect and select from Series and DataFrame objects
Filter rows with loc, iloc, Boolean masks and query
Convert dtypes deliberately and handle missing values with a reason
Clean duplicates, text, categories and outliers into a validated table
Read and write CSV, JSON, SQL and Parquet without losing types
Merge and concatenate datasets and prove the join did not fan out
Group, aggregate and reshape data into the table a question needs
Work with datetimes, resampling and rolling windows
Profile memory and process files larger than RAM in chunks
Prepare a leakage-free dataset for scikit-learn
Run a full EDA and explain the findings as a data analyst

modules.title: Pandas Foundations
modules.goal: Understand what Pandas is for, what a DataFrame is, and how it differs from a list, a NumPy array, Excel and SQL.

topics.title: What a DataFrame gives you
topics.body: A DataFrame is a table with named columns of different types. `shape` reports rows and columns; a column is a Series, so statistics are one method away.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

students = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Aman", "Riya", "Rahul"], "marks": [85, 92, 78]})
print(students.shape)
print(students["marks"].mean())

topics.title: A Series is one labelled column
topics.body: A Series pairs values with an index. Give it string labels and `.loc` reads by label instead of by position.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

marks = pd.Series([85, 92, 78], index=["Aman", "Riya", "Rahul"])
print(marks.loc["Riya"])
print(marks.max())

topics.title: Build a DataFrame from a dict
topics.body: Each dict key becomes a column and the values become its rows. This is the shape every CSV becomes after `read_csv`.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [120, 90]})
print(df.columns.tolist())
print(df["sales"].sum())

topics.title: Every DataFrame has an index
topics.body: Rows carry labels too. The default index is 0, 1, 2, and `.loc[1]` means the row labelled 1 — not the second row after a sort.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"sales": [120, 90, 60]})
print(df.index.tolist())
print(df.loc[1, "sales"])

topics.title: Lists concatenate, Series add
topics.body: `+` on two Python lists joins them; on two Series it adds element by element. That difference is the whole reason Pandas exists.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

print([1, 2] + [3, 4])
print((pd.Series([1, 2]) + pd.Series([3, 4])).tolist())

interviewBank.q: Why does Pandas exist when Python already has lists and NumPy has arrays?
interviewBank.answer: Lists and NumPy arrays are positional: column 0 means nothing. Pandas adds labelled rows and columns of mixed types, alignment by label, missing-value handling and grouping, which are the operations tabular analysis actually needs. NumPy is still underneath for the fast numeric path.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a Series and a DataFrame?
interviewBank.answer: A Series is one labelled, typed 1-D array — one column plus its index. A DataFrame is a dict-like collection of Series that share one index, so it is 2-D with named columns. `df["col"]` returns a Series; `df[["col"]]` returns a one-column DataFrame.

defenseBank.q: A teammate says "use Pandas, it is faster than Python loops". How do you answer precisely?
defenseBank.answer: Pandas is faster for column-wise work because operations run in compiled code over contiguous blocks. It is not faster automatically: `apply(axis=1)` and `iterrows` still run Python per row and can be slower than a plain loop. The speed comes from vectorised column operations, not from the word Pandas.
steps: Name the vectorised call that replaces the loop.
Say when a loop is still the right tool.

defenseBank.q: When would you choose Excel or SQL over Pandas?
defenseBank.answer: Excel when a non-programmer has to edit and review the sheet. SQL when the data already lives in a database and is too large to pull into memory. Pandas wins when the analysis needs code, reproducibility and joins across files.
steps: State who has to read the result.
State where the data lives and how big it is.
Name the reproducibility cost of the alternative.

modules.title: Series, DataFrame and Index
modules.goal: Create both structures from every common input and read their labels, axes and alignment rules.

topics.title: A custom index travels with the values
topics.body: The index is data, not decoration. `s["b"]` and `s.loc["b"]` both read by label, and the labels survive arithmetic.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=["a", "b", "c"])
print(s.index.tolist())
print(s.loc["b"])

topics.title: A list of dicts becomes rows
topics.body: Pandas unions the keys across records; a missing key becomes NaN rather than an error, which is how JSON arrays load.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

rows = [{"id": 1, "team": "core"}, {"id": 2}]
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(df.shape)
print(df["team"].isna().tolist())

topics.title: Index and columns are the two axes
topics.body: `axis=0` walks down the rows, `axis=1` walks across the columns. Every reduction and every `apply` takes one of them.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
print(df.sum(axis=0).tolist())
print(df.sum(axis=1).tolist())

topics.title: Arithmetic aligns by label
topics.body: Two Series add by matching index labels, not by position. Labels that exist on only one side become NaN unless you pass `fill_value`.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.Series([1, 2], index=["x", "y"])
b = pd.Series([10, 20], index=["y", "z"])
print(a.add(b, fill_value=0).tolist())

topics.title: Selecting one column versus many
topics.body: One column in double brackets stays a DataFrame, which is what `to_csv`, `merge` and most plotting calls expect.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1], "b": [2]})
print(type(df["a"]).__name__)
print(type(df[["a"]]).__name__)

tasks.title: Add two aligned Series
tasks.statement: Add the two Series by label so that missing labels count as zero, then print the total as a plain list.
tasks.solution:

a = pd.Series([5, 6], index=["p", "q"])
b = pd.Series([7], index=["q"])
print(a.add(b, fill_value=0).tolist())

interviewBank.q: What does index alignment mean, and where does it surprise people?
interviewBank.answer: When two pandas objects combine, rows are matched by index label rather than position. A filtered Series keeps its original labels, so adding it back to the full frame leaves NaN on the removed rows. Sorting or resetting the index first is the usual fix.

interviewBank.q: Why is `df['col']` sometimes a Series and sometimes a DataFrame?
interviewBank.answer: A single label returns the column as a Series; a list of labels returns a DataFrame with those columns. The bracket count is the type switch, which matters because `to_csv` and plotting helpers expect a frame.

defenseBank.q: Justify keeping a meaningful index instead of resetting to 0..n.
defenseBank.answer: A meaningful index makes label lookups and alignment explicit, and it keeps `merge` on the index cheap. Reset it when the label has no meaning or repeats — a duplicate index makes `.loc` return several rows and silently inflates joins.

defenseBank.q: A learner's table has 3 columns and 1,000 rows, and `df.sum()` returns one number per column. Explain the rule.

interview.q: What does index alignment mean, and where does it surprise people?
interview.answer: When two pandas objects combine, rows are matched by index label rather than position. A filtered Series keeps its original labels, so adding it back to the full frame leaves NaN on the removed rows. Sorting or resetting the index first is the usual fix.

interview.q: Why is `df['col']` sometimes a Series and sometimes a DataFrame?
interview.answer: A single label returns the column as a Series; a list of labels returns a DataFrame with those columns. The bracket count is the type switch, which matters because `to_csv` and plotting helpers expect a frame.

topics.title: head and tail show the edges
topics.body: `head(2)` and `tail(2)` preview the first and last rows without loading anything extra, which is the first thing to run on an unknown file.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3, 4], "marks": [80, 90, 70, 60]})
print(df.head(2)["id"].tolist())
print(df.tail(2)["id"].tolist())

topics.title: shape, size and ndim
topics.body: `shape` is (rows, columns), `size` is rows × columns, `ndim` is 2 for every DataFrame. Printing all three catches a wrong separator immediately.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
print(df.shape, df.size, df.ndim)

topics.title: dtypes are the contract
topics.body: A numeric column stored as text breaks every mean. `dtypes` shows the truth, and `object` or `str` on a number column is the warning sign.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "name": ["a", "b"], "fee": [10.5, 20.0]})
print(df.dtypes.astype(str).tolist())

topics.title: describe summarises every numeric column
topics.body: `describe()` returns count, mean, std, min, quartiles and max in one call. Comparing mean and median there is the fastest skew check.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"marks": [10, 20, 30, 40]})
print(df["marks"].describe().round(1).tolist())

topics.title: value_counts answers what is in a column
topics.body: `value_counts` counts each distinct value, sorted by frequency. `nunique` gives just the number of distinct values.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"]})
print(df["city"].value_counts().to_dict())
print(df["city"].nunique())

interviewBank.q: You open a CSV and every column is `object`. What do you check first?
interviewBank.answer: Whether the file parsed at all: a wrong separator, a header row inside the data or thousands separators turn numbers into text. `df.head()` plus `df.dtypes` tells you which, then re-read with the right `sep`, `thousands` or `dtype`.

interviewBank.q: What does `describe()` hide that a histogram would not?
interviewBank.answer: Shape. Mean, std and quartiles can be identical for a bimodal column and a normal one, and they say nothing about gaps, spikes or a hard cap. Plot or bin the column before trusting the summary.

defenseBank.q: Argue for profiling a dataset before writing any cleaning code.
defenseBank.answer: Cleaning decisions depend on facts the profile supplies: which columns are text, where missing values sit, whether a category is consistent. Cleaning first means guessing, and a guess like filling a numeric gap with 0 can be wrong for the domain.
steps: Name the facts a profile returns.
Name one decision each fact changes.

defenseBank.q: When is `value_counts` the wrong tool?
defenseBank.answer: On a high-cardinality column such as an id or a free-text field: nearly every value is unique, so the table is long and uninformative. Use `nunique`, a head/tail of the counts, or bin the column first.
steps: Say what the output looks like.

modules.title: Selection, Indexing and Filtering
modules.goal: Read any cell, row, column or subset by label, position or condition — and know which one you used.

topics.title: loc selects by label
topics.body: `df.loc[row_label, column_label]` always means labels, and slices include the stop label — the opposite of a Python list slice.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"marks": [85, 92, 78]}, index=["a", "b", "c"])
print(df.loc["b", "marks"])
print(df.loc["a":"b", "marks"].tolist())

topics.title: iloc selects by position
topics.body: `df.iloc[0, 1]` is first row, second column. Slices exclude the stop, like Python. Use it when there is no meaningful label.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Aman", "Riya"], "marks": [85, 92]})
print(df.iloc[0, 1])
print(df.iloc[:, 0].tolist())

topics.title: A Boolean mask keeps the True rows
topics.body: A comparison returns a same-shape mask; putting it inside the brackets filters the rows. The result keeps the original index labels.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Aman", "Riya", "Rahul"], "marks": [85, 92, 78]})
print(df[df["marks"] > 80]["name"].tolist())
print(df[df["marks"] > 80].index.tolist())

topics.title: query reads like a condition
topics.body: `query` takes a string, so `and`/`or` work and the condition can come from a config value. Column names with spaces need backticks.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Aman", "Riya"], "marks": [85, 92]})
print(df.query("marks > 80")["name"].tolist())
print(df.query("marks > 80").shape[0])

topics.title: isin and between test a range or a set
topics.body: `isin` answers "is this value in my list", `between` answers "is it inside this interval". Both return masks that combine with `&`.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Delhi"], "marks": [85, 70]})
print(df["city"].isin(["Pune"]).tolist())
print(df["marks"].between(80, 95).tolist())

print(df[(df["city"] == "Pune") & (df["marks"] >= 80)]["name"].tolist())

interviewBank.q: What is the practical difference between loc and iloc?
interviewBank.answer: loc uses labels and includes the stop of a slice; iloc uses 0-based positions and excludes it. The trap is that a default RangeIndex makes them look identical until a filter or sort reorders the labels.

interviewBank.q: Why is chained assignment risky, and what replaces it?
interviewBank.answer: `df[df.a > 1]["b"] = 0` may write into a temporary copy, so the original frame never changes. The supported form is one `.loc` call: `df.loc[df.a > 1, "b"] = 0`, which writes into the frame itself.

defenseBank.q: A query returns 0 rows and no error. Walk through how you would debug it.
defenseBank.answer: Check the dtype being compared (text "85" never exceeds 80), check for whitespace or case in a string category, print the mask's sum to see if it is all False, and confirm the column name exists with `df.columns`. A silent empty frame is always a comparison that never matched.
steps: Print dtype and a sample value.

defenseBank.q: Explain why filtering keeps the old index, and when you would reset it.
defenseBank.answer: Filtering selects rows, so their labels travel with them; the gaps are information that the row came from position 7. Reset when the index is about to be used positionally, exported, or merged, because duplicate or gapped labels confuse `.loc`.
steps: Say what the label means after filtering.

modules.title: Data Types and Conversion
modules.goal: Read a dtype, choose the right one, and convert without turning bad values into silent garbage.

topics.title: astype changes the stored type
topics.body: `astype` converts between compatible types and raises on values it cannot represent. It is the explicit way to make an integer column a float.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])
print(s.dtype)
print(s.astype(float).dtype)

topics.title: to_numeric can coerce bad values
topics.body: `pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce")` turns unparseable entries into NaN instead of raising, which is how a dirty price column becomes usable.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

raw = pd.Series(["10", "x", "30"])
clean = pd.to_numeric(raw, errors="coerce")
print(clean.isna().sum())
print(clean.fillna(0).tolist())

topics.title: to_datetime parses dates once
topics.body: Parsing at load time makes `.dt` available and turns comparisons into date comparisons. `errors="coerce"` puts invalid dates into NaT.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

dates = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(["2026-01-05", "2026-02-10"]))
print(dates.dt.month.tolist())
print((dates.dt.dayofweek < 5).tolist())

topics.title: convert_dtypes picks nullable types
topics.body: `convert_dtypes` chooses the nullable extension types, so an integer column with a gap becomes `Int64` instead of silently turning into floats.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, None, 3])
print(s.dtype)
print(s.convert_dtypes().dtype)

topics.title: category pays off on repeats
topics.body: A category stores each distinct string once plus integer codes. Memory drops sharply when a column repeats a few values across many rows.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

text = pd.Series(["pune", "delhi"] * 500)
packed = text.astype("category")
print(packed.dtype)
print(packed.cat.categories.tolist())

interviewBank.q: Why does an integer column with one missing value become float?
interviewBank.answer: The classic int64 dtype has no NaN representation, so pandas promotes the column to float64 to hold the gap. The nullable `Int64` extension dtype keeps integers and stores missing as `pd.NA`, which is what `convert_dtypes` selects.

interviewBank.q: When does `category` hurt instead of help?
interviewBank.answer: When the column is nearly unique: codes plus a large category array cost more than object pointers. It also complicates operations that need arbitrary values, and adding a new category has to update the dtype. It wins with a small, repeated vocabulary.

defenseBank.q: Argue for converting dtypes at load time rather than after cleaning.
defenseBank.answer: Typed data fails loudly and cheaply: `parse_dates` or `dtype=` makes a wrong file fail at the boundary instead of at the groupby. It also avoids the float promotion trap and keeps memory predictable from the first line.

defenseBank.q: An analyst says "just use errors='coerce' everywhere". What is the risk?
defenseBank.answer: Coercion hides the cause: a wrongly specified decimal separator turns every value into NaN and the analysis reports zero without an error. Coerce, then count and inspect the NaNs it created before continuing.

interviewBank.q: When is `apply` the right call?
interviewBank.answer: When the logic is genuinely row-wise and irregular — a lookup across several columns with branching, or a call into library code that takes a row. Even then, `axis=1` is slow; if the operation can be expressed as column arithmetic, that version wins.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between `map`, `apply` and `transform` on a Series?
interviewBank.answer: `map` substitutes values (dict, Series or function) elementwise and returns the same shape. `apply` can return an aggregate, so its shape may change. `transform` guarantees the original shape, which is what you need when feeding the result back into the frame.

defenseBank.q: Defend this claim: a calculated column should never overwrite its input.
defenseBank.answer: Overwriting destroys the raw value, so a wrong formula cannot be recomputed or audited, and a downstream bug becomes unrecoverable. Keep the input and write the result under a new name; drop the raw column at export if it is genuinely redundant.
steps: State what is lost on overwrite.

defenseBank.q: Your percentage column has inf values and the dashboard shows blank cells. Explain the chain and the fix.
defenseBank.answer: Dividing by zero produces inf, and a later JSON or chart step cannot represent it, so it disappears. Replace the zero denominator with NaN before dividing, then decide explicitly whether to fill, drop or flag those rows.
steps: Name the step that loses it.

modules.goal: Order a table, rank inside groups, and read the right descriptive statistic for the question.

topics.title: sort_values orders rows
topics.body: `sort_values` returns a new frame unless `inplace=True`. The index travels with the row, which is why a sorted frame often has an out-of-order index.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["Aman", "Riya", "Rahul"], "marks": [85, 92, 78]})
print(df.sort_values("marks", ascending=False)["name"].tolist())

topics.title: Two sort keys, two directions
topics.body: Pass a list of columns and a matching list of booleans. The first key dominates; the second breaks ties.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "marks": [70, 90, 95]})
out = df.sort_values(["city", "marks"], ascending=[True, False])

modules.title: Missing Data
modules.goal: Find missing values, understand why they are missing, and choose a handling strategy you can defend.

topics.title: isna counts the gaps per column
topics.body: `isna()` returns a boolean frame of the same shape, so summing it gives one count per column and the percentage is one division away.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None], "b": [None, None]})
print(df.isna().sum().tolist())
print(round(df.isna().mean().max() * 100, 1))

topics.title: dropna removes rows by rule
topics.body: With no arguments it drops any row containing a gap; `subset` limits the rule to the columns the analysis actually needs.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "marks": [80, None, 70]})
print(df.dropna().shape[0])
print(df.dropna(subset=["id"]).shape[0])

topics.title: fillna with a decided value
topics.body: Filling with the mean keeps the count and the mean, but shrinks the variance. State which one the analysis needs before choosing the fill value.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10.0, None, 30.0])
print(s.fillna(s.mean()).tolist())
print(s.isna().sum())

topics.title: ffill carries the last known value
topics.body: `ffill` copies the previous non-missing value forward, which is correct for a status that only changes when a new event arrives — not for a measurement.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["active", None, None, "paused"])
print(s.ffill().tolist())

topics.title: interpolate estimates between points
topics.body: Linear interpolation draws a straight line between known values. It suits a smooth series such as temperature, and invents data in a sparse one.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10.0, None, 30.0])
print(s.interpolate().tolist())

interviewBank.q: What are the three kinds of missingness, and why does the kind matter?
interviewBank.answer: MCAR (random), MAR (explained by other columns) and MNAR (explained by the missing value itself, such as high earners skipping a salary field). Dropping is safe only under MCAR; otherwise the missingness is signal and should be modelled, for example with a fill plus an `is_missing` flag.

interviewBank.q: Why is filling with the mean often the weakest choice?
interviewBank.answer: It reduces variance, distorts correlations and creates a spike at one value, while pretending the estimate is a real measurement. Median or model-based fills are more robust, and an explicit missing indicator is often more honest than any fill.

defenseBank.q: A column is 60% missing. Defend your plan.
defenseBank.answer: Above roughly half missing, an imputed column mostly encodes the imputation rule, so I would first check whether the record exists at all (a status or an all-null block). If it does, keep it with an explicit missing flag and exclude it from any average that would be dominated by the fill.
steps: Check whether the gap is structural.
Keep the flag, exclude from averages.

defenseBank.q: Explain why ffill is right for a status column and wrong for a temperature column.
defenseBank.answer: A status is a state that persists until the next event, so the last known value is the true value. A temperature changes continuously, so carrying the last reading forward invents a plateau and understates the variation.

interview.q: What are the three kinds of missingness, and why does the kind matter?
interview.answer: MCAR (random), MAR (explained by other columns) and MNAR (explained by the missing value itself, such as high earners skipping a salary field). Dropping is safe only under MCAR; otherwise the missingness is signal and should be modelled, for example with a fill plus an `is_missing` flag.

interview.q: Why is filling with the mean often the weakest choice?
interview.answer: It reduces variance, distorts correlations and creates a spike at one value, while pretending the estimate is a real measurement. Median or model-based fills are more robust, and an explicit missing indicator is often more honest than any fill.

defense.q: A column is 60% missing. Defend your plan.
defense.answer: Above roughly half missing, an imputed column mostly encodes the imputation rule, so I would first check whether the record exists at all (a status or an all-null block). If it does, keep it with an explicit missing flag and exclude it from any average that would be dominated by the fill.

defense.q: Explain why ffill is right for a status column and wrong for a temperature column.
defense.answer: A status is a state that persists until the next event, so the last known value is the true value. A temperature changes continuously, so carrying the last reading forward invents a plateau and understates the variation.

modules.title: Cleaning and Validation
modules.goal: Turn a messy table into a validated one: duplicates, names, categories, whitespace and outliers.

topics.title: drop_duplicates keeps one row per record
topics.body: `duplicated()` marks repeats after the first. `drop_duplicates` removes them, optionally only when a subset of the columns matches.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 1, 2], "v": [10, 10, 20]})
print(df.duplicated().tolist())
print(df.drop_duplicates().shape[0])

topics.title: rename fixes column names
topics.body: `rename(columns={...})` changes labels without touching data, which is how a raw export becomes a table the rest of the code can name.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"Student Name": ["Aman"], "Marks Obtained": [85]})
df = df.rename(columns={"Student Name": "name", "Marks Obtained": "marks"})
print(df.columns.tolist())

topics.title: replace standardises values
topics.body: A dict maps several spellings onto one canonical value. Without it, groupby treats "Pune" and "pune " as two different cities.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "pune ", "PUNE"]})
df["city"] = df["city"].str.strip().str.lower().replace({"pune": "Pune"})
print(df["city"].tolist())

topics.title: Whitespace hides in the middle of a category
topics.body: Trailing spaces survive every comparison, filter and join. Strip the whole column before anything else looks at it.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"name": [" Aman", "Riya "]})
print(df["name"].str.len().tolist())
print(df["name"].str.strip().str.len().tolist())

topics.title: IQR flags outliers by position
topics.body: The IQR rule marks values outside Q1 − 1.5·IQR and Q3 + 1.5·IQR. It is robust to a few extremes because quartiles ignore the tail.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10, 12, 11, 13, 100])
q1, q3 = s.quantile(0.25), s.quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1
print(s[(s < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (s > q3 + 1.5 * iqr)].tolist())

interviewBank.q: How do you decide which duplicate to keep?
interviewBank.answer: By the grain and by the newest record: typically order by an updated-at column and keep the last per key. Keeping the first silently keeps the oldest state, which is wrong for slowly changing records.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between an outlier and an invalid value?
interviewBank.answer: An outlier is a real observation far from the rest; an invalid value is impossible — a negative age, a date in the future, a price of zero on a paid order. Validation rules catch the impossible; statistics only flag the unusual.

defenseBank.q: Defend writing a validation report before removing any row.
defenseBank.answer: Removal is irreversible and hides the cause. A report that counts duplicates, invalid values and outliers per column shows whether the pipeline is broken upstream, and gives a number to compare after the fix instead of a silently smaller table.

defenseBank.q: A teammate drops every row outside 3 standard deviations. What is the problem?
defenseBank.answer: The rule assumes a roughly normal distribution and is itself distorted by the extreme values it targets; on a skewed column it can delete a large legitimate tail. Use IQR or a domain threshold, and say which rows were removed.

defense.q: Defend writing a validation report before removing any row.
defense.answer: Removal is irreversible and hides the cause. A report that counts duplicates, invalid values and outliers per column shows whether the pipeline is broken upstream, and gives a number to compare after the fix instead of a silently smaller table.

defense.q: A teammate drops every row outside 3 standard deviations. What is the problem?
defense.answer: The rule assumes a roughly normal distribution and is itself distorted by the extreme values it targets; on a skewed column it can delete a large legitimate tail. Use IQR or a domain threshold, and say which rows were removed.

modules.title: Strings and Regular Expressions
modules.goal: Clean and extract text with the .str accessor and regex, without a Python loop.

topics.title: str.contains filters text
topics.body: `contains` returns a boolean mask; `case=False` and `regex=True` are the two arguments that decide whether a search is literal or a pattern.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"email": ["a@gmail.com", "b@yahoo.com"]})
print(df["email"].str.contains("gmail", case=False).tolist())

topics.title: str.extract pulls a group out
topics.body: A capture group in the pattern becomes a column. `expand=False` returns a Series when there is exactly one group.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"email": ["a@gmail.com", "b@yahoo.com"]})
df["domain"] = df["email"].str.extract(r"@(\w+)\.")
print(df["domain"].tolist())

topics.title: str.split expands into columns
topics.body: `split(pat, expand=True)` turns one text column into several, which is how a "city, state" field becomes two usable columns.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"where": ["Pune, MH", "Delhi, DL"]})
parts = df["where"].str.split(", ", expand=True)
print(parts.shape)
print(parts[0].tolist())

topics.title: str.len measures the text
topics.body: Length is a cheap validation: a phone number column with lengths other than 10 is wrong before any regex.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"phone": ["9876543210", "98765"]})
print(df["phone"].str.len().tolist())

topics.title: Regex cleans a phone number
topics.body: `replace` with `regex=True` removes every non-digit in one pass, then the length check tells you which numbers are still invalid.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"phone": ["+91 98765-43210", "(022) 1234 5678"]})
digits = df["phone"].str.replace(r"\D", "", regex=True)
print(digits.str.len().tolist())

interviewBank.q: Why prefer a vectorised .str call over a list comprehension of string methods?
interviewBank.answer: The `.str` accessor handles missing values as NaN instead of raising, runs the same compiled loop over the column, and keeps the index. A comprehension needs its own None handling and rebuilds a Series.

interviewBank.q: When is a regex the wrong tool?
interviewBank.answer: When the format is structured — parse JSON, split on a fixed delimiter, or use a real date parser. Regex for HTML or nested syntax becomes unreadable and wrong at the edges; use the parser that owns the format.

defenseBank.q: Defend normalising text before grouping.
defenseBank.answer: Group keys compare exactly, so "Pune", "pune" and "Pune " become three groups and every aggregate is split three ways. Normalising case and whitespace first makes the group count match the real number of cities.

defenseBank.q: A phone column has 8, 10 and 12 digit values. What do you report?
defenseBank.answer: That the column has three length populations, which usually means a country code or a missing prefix, not bad data. Report the counts per length before changing anything, then normalise with an explicit rule.

topics.title: read_csv with an explicit separator
topics.body: `read_csv` splits on a comma by default. A semicolon or tab file that is not declared arrives as one wide text column.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

text = "name;marks\nAman;85\nRiya;92"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(text), sep=";")
print(df.shape)
print(df["marks"].sum())

topics.title: Read only the columns you need
topics.body: `usecols` and `dtype` cut memory at the source: a wide export becomes a small typed frame without a post-load clean-up.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

text = "id,name,marks\n1,Aman,85\n2,Riya,92"
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(text), usecols=["name", "marks"], dtype={"marks": "int16"})
print(df.columns.tolist())
print(df["marks"].dtype)

topics.title: to_csv without the index
topics.body: By default the index is written as an unnamed first column. `index=False` is what stops a round trip from growing a column each time.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]})
print(df.to_csv(index=False).strip().split("\n"))

topics.title: JSON arrives as records
topics.body: A JSON array of objects becomes rows directly; nested objects need `json_normalize` to become columns.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

records = [{"id": 1, "meta": {"city": "Pune"}}, {"id": 2, "meta": {"city": "Delhi"}}]
df = pd.json_normalize(records)
print(df.columns.tolist())

topics.title: read_sql runs inside the database
topics.body: `read_sql` sends the query and builds the frame from the result, so filtering happens in SQL instead of after a full load.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("create table marks (name text, mark integer)")
con.executemany("insert into marks values (?, ?)", [("Aman", 85), ("Riya", 92)])
print(pd.read_sql("select name from marks where mark > 90", con)["name"].tolist())

interviewBank.q: How do you read a 20 GB CSV on a laptop?
interviewBank.answer: In chunks: `read_csv(..., chunksize=1_000_000)` and aggregate each chunk into a small result, so peak memory is one chunk. If the file is columnar, convert once to Parquet and read only the needed columns.

interviewBank.q: What does `parse_dates` change about later work?
interviewBank.answer: It makes the column datetime64, which enables `.dt`, resampling, rolling windows and date arithmetic. Without it the column is text, comparisons are lexicographic and `resample` raises.

defenseBank.q: Argue for pinning a dtype map in a production loader.
defenseBank.answer: An inferred dtype can change when the data changes — one new blank cell turns an integer column into float and the join key stops matching. An explicit map makes the contract fail at load instead of at analysis.

defenseBank.q: When is exporting to CSV the wrong deliverable?
defenseBank.answer: When the consumer is another program that needs types and speed, or when the data is large: CSV loses dtypes, is slow to parse and cannot hold nested or binary values. Parquet keeps the schema and reads only the columns asked for.

modules.title: Merging, Joining and Concatenation
modules.goal: Combine tables by key or by stacking, and prove the row count did what you intended.

topics.title: merge joins on a shared key
topics.body: `merge` matches rows by key and keeps the columns of both sides. The default `how="inner"` keeps only keys present in both.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

users = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "name": ["Aman", "Riya"]})
marks = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 3], "mark": [85, 92]})
print(users.merge(marks, on="id").shape[0])

topics.title: A left join keeps every row on the left
topics.body: `how="left"` never drops a left row; unmatched keys get NaN on the right. That is the shape of a "who has not done it" question.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

users = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "name": ["Aman", "Riya"]})
marks = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1], "mark": [85]})
out = users.merge(marks, on="id", how="left")
print(out["mark"].isna().tolist())

topics.title: indicator names where each row came from
topics.body: `indicator=True` adds `_merge` with `both`, `left_only` or `right_only`, which turns an audit question into a filter.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"id": [2, 3]})
out = a.merge(b, on="id", how="outer", indicator=True)
print(out["_merge"].value_counts().to_dict())

topics.title: concat stacks rows
topics.body: `concat` glues tables along an axis without matching keys. `ignore_index=True` renumbers the result so the old labels do not repeat.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

jan = pd.DataFrame({"sales": [10]})
feb = pd.DataFrame({"sales": [20]})
out = pd.concat([jan, feb], ignore_index=True)
print(out["sales"].tolist())
print(out.index.tolist())

topics.title: validate refuses a fan-out
topics.body: A duplicate key on either side multiplies rows. `validate="one_to_one"` raises instead of shipping a table that is quietly bigger.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "x": [10, 20]})
b = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "y": [1, 2]})
print(a.merge(b, on="id", validate="one_to_one").shape[0])

interviewBank.q: Why does a merge sometimes return more rows than the left table?
interviewBank.answer: Because the key is not unique on the right: each match produces a row, so one left row with three right matches becomes three. That is a fan-out, and `validate` is the check that catches it before the numbers are trusted.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between merge and join?
interviewBank.answer: `merge` is the general, key-based operation with `on`, `how` and `validate`. `join` is a convenience that joins on the index by default. For anything beyond a simple index join, `merge` is the explicit choice.

defenseBank.q: Explain why you check the row count before and after every join.
defenseBank.answer: A join can multiply or drop rows without any error. Comparing counts before and after is the cheapest proof that the relationship was what I assumed, and when it changes I know the key is not unique.

defenseBank.q: When is concat the right tool instead of merge?
defenseBank.answer: When the tables are the same shape and represent the same entity over time or source — monthly files, two regions. Merge combines different attributes of one entity; concat extends the rows of one table.

topics.title: groupby splits, then aggregates
topics.body: `groupby(key)` groups rows with the same key; a reduction then returns one value per group instead of per row.

topics.title: agg asks several questions at once
topics.body: Passing a list of function names returns one column per function. Named aggregation gives those columns the names the report needs.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})

topics.title: transform keeps the row count
topics.body: `transform` returns a value per original row, so a group mean can be attached back and used in a per-row comparison.

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})

print(df["avg"].tolist())

topics.title: filter keeps whole groups
topics.body: `filter` takes a function of the group and returns the rows of the groups that pass, which is different from filtering rows.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
out = df.groupby("city").filter(lambda g: g["sales"].sum() > 20)
print(out["city"].unique().tolist())

topics.title: Two keys make a MultiIndex result
topics.body: Grouping by two columns returns a Series indexed by both keys. `unstack` turns the second key into columns for a report.

interviewBank.q: What does groupby actually do internally?
interviewBank.answer: Split the rows into groups by the key, apply the function to each group, combine the results into one object indexed by the key. The split is why a groupby on a high-cardinality key is expensive, and why the result is indexed by that key.

interviewBank.q: When do you use transform instead of agg?
interviewBank.answer: When the answer must line up with the original rows: adding a group mean to each row, or comparing a row against its group. `agg` collapses each group to one row; `transform` returns one value per input row.

defenseBank.q: A groupby mean looks wrong because one group has a single row. What do you do?
defenseBank.answer: Report the group size beside the mean, because a mean of one observation has no spread and is not comparable. Filter or flag groups below a minimum count, and say the threshold in the output.

defenseBank.q: Explain the difference between dropping missing keys and keeping them in a groupby.
defenseBank.answer: By default `groupby` drops rows whose key is missing, so the totals silently shrink. `dropna=False` keeps them as a group, which is right when the missing key itself is a finding.
steps: Give the flag and when to use it.

topics.title: pivot_table builds a cross-tab
topics.body: `pivot_table` aggregates by default, so duplicate key combinations do not raise. Rows, columns and values are named explicitly.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "year": [2025, 2026, 2026], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
t = df.pivot_table(index="city", columns="year", values="sales", aggfunc="sum")
print(t.shape)
print(t.loc["Pune"].tolist())

topics.title: melt turns columns into rows
topics.body: `melt` is the inverse of a pivot: wide columns become a key column plus a value column, which is the shape plotting and groupby prefer.

interviewBank.q: When do you want long data instead of wide?
interviewBank.answer: When the analysis groups or plots by a variable that is currently spread across columns — year, metric, region. Long data has one value column and one key column, which is what groupby, seaborn and most model APIs expect.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between pivot and pivot_table?
interviewBank.answer: `pivot` only reshapes unique index/column pairs and raises on duplicates. `pivot_table` aggregates duplicates with `aggfunc`, so it is the safe choice on real data.

defenseBank.q: Defend storing a clean dataset in long format.
defenseBank.answer: Long format is additive: a new month is new rows, not a new column, so no code or schema changes. It also makes the metric a value instead of a column name, which is what groupby and plotting need.

defenseBank.q: A pivot table has a NaN where you expect a zero. Explain and fix.
defenseBank.answer: The combination simply does not exist in the data, so there is no row to aggregate and pandas leaves NaN. `fill_value=0` states the business meaning — no activity — instead of implying unknown.
steps: Say why the cell is NaN.

modules.title: Datetime and Time Series
modules.goal: Parse dates, extract parts, resample a series and compute rolling windows.

topics.title: Parse once, then use dt
topics.body: `to_datetime` makes the column datetime64, and the `.dt` accessor then exposes year, month, weekday and formatting without another parse.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"at": ["2026-01-05", "2026-02-10"]})
df["at"] = pd.to_datetime(df["at"])
print(df["at"].dt.month.tolist())
print(df["at"].dt.day_name().tolist())

topics.title: date_range generates the calendar
topics.body: `date_range` builds an index of dates with a frequency. `freq="W"` marks weekly boundaries and `"B"` business days, which is how a gap-free series is built.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

idx = pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=3, freq="D")
print(idx.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist())

topics.title: resample aggregates by period
topics.body: With a DatetimeIndex, `resample("M")` groups rows into months and applies a reduction — the time-series version of groupby.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

idx = pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-05", "2026-01-20", "2026-02-02"])
s = pd.Series([10, 20, 5], index=idx)
print(s.resample("MS").sum().tolist())

topics.title: rolling smooths a series
topics.body: `rolling(2).mean()` averages each point with the previous one. The first window is incomplete, so it starts as NaN.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10.0, 20.0, 30.0])
print(s.rolling(2).mean().round(1).tolist())

topics.title: shift compares with the previous period
topics.body: `shift(1)` moves values down one row, so subtracting it gives the change from the previous period without a loop.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([100, 110, 99])
print(s.diff().tolist())

import pandas as pd

print(s.resample("MS").sum().tolist())

s = pd.Series([1, 2], index=pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01", "2026-02-01"]))
print(s.resample("MS").sum().tolist())

interviewBank.q: Why is resampling different from groupby on a month column?
interviewBank.answer: Resample knows the calendar: it produces every period in the range, including empty ones, and respects frequency rules such as business days and month starts. Grouping on an extracted month only returns the months that exist.

interviewBank.q: What does `rolling(7)` do at the start of a series?
interviewBank.answer: The first six windows are incomplete, so the default result is NaN. `min_periods=1` computes with whatever is available, which changes the shape of the early values and should be a stated decision.

defenseBank.q: Defend converting to datetime at load rather than when a chart needs it.
defenseBank.answer: The parse either succeeds once or fails once, at the boundary, with one dtype for the column. Parsing later means every consumer has to remember, and mixed formats can parse differently in two places.

defenseBank.q: A monthly revenue chart shows a dip every February. How do you explain it?
defenseBank.answer: February is shorter, so a monthly sum compares unequal periods. Compare a daily average, or use a same-length window or year-over-year comparison before calling it a decline.

modules.title: Advanced Pandas
modules.goal: Use MultiIndex, categoricals, pipelines and index alignment deliberately instead of avoiding them.

topics.title: A MultiIndex is a key of several levels
topics.body: Grouping by two keys produces a MultiIndex. `get_level_values` reads one level back as a flat index.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "year": [2025, 2026, 2026], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
s = df.groupby(["city", "year"])["sales"].sum()
print(s.index.nlevels)
print(s.index.get_level_values("year").tolist())

topics.title: xs selects one level
topics.body: `xs` cross-sections a MultiIndex at one level, returning the remaining levels without a full reset.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "year": [2025, 2026, 2026], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
s = df.groupby(["city", "year"])["sales"].sum()
print(s.xs(2026, level="year").tolist())

topics.title: Categorical makes the order explicit
topics.body: A categorical dtype knows its categories and whether order matters, so sorting and plotting follow the domain order instead of alphabetical.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["medium", "low", "high"], dtype=pd.CategoricalDtype(["low", "medium", "high"], ordered=True))
print(s.sort_values().tolist())

topics.title: pipe keeps a pipeline readable
topics.body: `pipe` passes the frame into a function, so a sequence of named steps reads top to bottom instead of nesting calls.

topics.title: combine_first fills holes from another table
topics.body: `combine_first` takes the first non-missing value across two aligned tables, which is how a corrected override is merged over a base record.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.Series([1.0, None, 3.0])
b = pd.Series([9.0, 2.0, 9.0])
print(a.combine_first(b).tolist())

interviewBank.q: What problem does a MultiIndex solve, and what does it cost?
interviewBank.answer: It keeps several key levels without repeating values or inventing a concatenated string key, and it supports cross-sections with `xs`. The cost is verbosity: most operations need `reset_index` or `level=` to be explicit, and a partially selected frame can surprise a reader.

interviewBank.q: Why is `pipe` better than one long chained expression?
interviewBank.answer: Each step becomes a named function that can be tested alone, and the reader sees the order of transformations. A chain of `.assign` and `.query` is fine until a step needs branching or a docstring.

defenseBank.q: Defend using categoricals for a status column.
defenseBank.answer: Status has a small fixed vocabulary, so codes save memory and the ordered categories make sorting and plotting correct. The constraint also fails loudly when a new value arrives instead of silently widening the column.

defenseBank.q: A pipeline has eight chained methods. When do you split it?
defenseBank.answer: When a step needs a comment longer than its name, when it is reused by another report, or when it is the only step that needs a test. Those are the points where a named function with `pipe` pays for itself.

interview.q: What problem does a MultiIndex solve, and what does it cost?
interview.answer: It keeps several key levels without repeating values or inventing a concatenated string key, and it supports cross-sections with `xs`. The cost is verbosity: most operations need `reset_index` or `level=` to be explicit, and a partially selected frame can surprise a reader.

interview.q: Why is `pipe` better than one long chained expression?
interview.answer: Each step becomes a named function that can be tested alone, and the reader sees the order of transformations. A chain of `.assign` and `.query` is fine until a step needs branching or a docstring.

modules.title: Exploratory Data Analysis
modules.goal: Profile a dataset, find the patterns worth reporting, and turn each one into a sentence a stakeholder can act on.

topics.title: Start with the distribution, not the mean
topics.body: Mean, median, std and quartiles together describe shape. A mean far above the median is the first sign of a long right tail.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"spend": [100, 120, 130, 900]})
print(round(df["spend"].mean(), 1), df["spend"].median())
print(round(df["spend"].quantile(0.75), 1))

topics.title: Value counts reveal the busy categories
topics.body: Counting a category before grouping tells you which groups are large enough to compare and which are noise.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"course": ["Python", "Python", "SQL", "Python"]})
counts = df["course"].value_counts()
print(counts.to_dict())
print(round(counts.max() / counts.sum() * 100, 1))

topics.title: Correlation is a starting question
topics.body: A correlation matrix ranks candidate relationships. Read it as "what to plot next", never as a finding on its own.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"hours": [1, 2, 3, 4], "marks": [40, 50, 65, 80], "sleep": [8, 7, 7, 6]})

topics.title: Group by the dimension in the question
topics.body: An EDA finding is usually a comparison: this segment versus that one. Group by the segment and report count plus rate, never a bare average.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "passed": [True, False, True]})
out = df.groupby("city")["passed"].agg(["count", "mean"])
print(out.loc["Pune"].round(2).tolist())

topics.title: cut turns a number into a band
topics.body: `cut` bins a continuous column into labelled intervals, which is how an age or spend distribution becomes a readable table.

bands = pd.cut(ages, bins=[0, 18, 35, 60, 100], labels=["teen", "young", "adult", "senior"])
print(bands.value_counts().to_dict())

interviewBank.q: Walk through your first fifteen minutes with an unknown dataset.
interviewBank.answer: Shape and dtypes, then missing counts and duplicates, then value counts for categories and `describe` for numerics, then a correlation look at the numeric columns. Each step decides the next question, and anything surprising becomes a note for the report.

interviewBank.q: How do you avoid reporting a correlation that is really a group effect?
interviewBank.answer: Check the relationship inside each segment as well as overall. Simpson's paradox is exactly this: a positive overall trend can reverse inside every group when the groups differ in size and level.

defenseBank.q: Defend reporting a median and a p95 instead of a mean.
defenseBank.answer: The mean is pulled by the tail and answers "total divided by count", which no user experiences. The median describes the typical case and p95 describes the worst case that still matters, which is what a decision usually needs.

defenseBank.q: A stakeholder asks for "the average engagement". What do you clarify first?
defenseBank.answer: The grain and the denominator: average per user, per session or per day, and whether a user with no activity counts as zero. Those three choices can change the number by an order of magnitude.

defense.q: Defend reporting a median and a p95 instead of a mean.
defense.answer: The mean is pulled by the tail and answers "total divided by count", which no user experiences. The median describes the typical case and p95 describes the worst case that still matters, which is what a decision usually needs.

defense.q: A stakeholder asks for "the average engagement". What do you clarify first?
defense.answer: The grain and the denominator: average per user, per session or per day, and whether a user with no activity counts as zero. Those three choices can change the number by an order of magnitude.

modules.title: Performance and Large Data
modules.goal: Measure memory, choose compact dtypes, and process data that does not fit in memory.

topics.title: memory_usage shows what a column costs
topics.body: `memory_usage(deep=True)` measures the real cost, including object pointers. It is the number to quote before optimising.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["pune", "delhi"] * 100)
print(s.memory_usage(deep=True) > 0)
print(s.astype("category").memory_usage(deep=True) < s.memory_usage(deep=True))

topics.title: Downcast a numeric column
topics.body: An int64 column of small values can be int16. `astype` halves or quarters the memory without changing the values.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="int64")
print(s.nbytes)
print(s.astype("int16").nbytes)

topics.title: Vectorised beats iterrows
topics.body: `iterrows` boxes every row into a Series, which is slow. A column expression does the same work in one compiled pass.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
print((df["a"] + df["b"]).tolist())

topics.title: Chunk a file that is too large
topics.body: `chunksize` returns an iterator of frames. Aggregating each chunk keeps peak memory at one chunk instead of the whole file.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

text = "v\n1\n2\n3\n4"
total = 0
for chunk in pd.read_csv(StringIO(text), chunksize=2):
    total += int(chunk["v"].sum())
print(total)

topics.title: eval avoids a temporary frame
topics.body: `eval` computes an expression without materialising each intermediate column, which matters when a pipeline chains several arithmetic steps.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
print(df.eval("a + b").tolist())

debug.title: Measuring with the default shallow memory
debug.broken:

print(s.memory_usage() == s.astype("category").memory_usage())
debug.fix:

debug.title: Mutating rows while iterating
debug.broken:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]})
for _, row in df.iterrows():
    row["a"] = row["a"] * 2
print(df["a"].tolist())
debug.fix:

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]})
df["a"] = df["a"] * 2
print(df["a"].tolist())
debug.error: Wrong output: [1, 2] — assigning into the row Series never writes back to the frame.

interviewBank.q: Where does Pandas actually get slow?
interviewBank.answer: Row-wise Python work: `iterrows`, `apply(axis=1)` and per-group Python functions. Column operations run in compiled code, so the wins come from rewriting a row loop as column arithmetic or a groupby aggregation.

interviewBank.q: When should you stop using Pandas?
interviewBank.answer: When the working set no longer fits comfortably in memory, or when a single machine cannot finish in the time budget. Then move to chunked processing for a one-off, or to a query engine, Parquet plus DuckDB, or a distributed tool when it is recurring.

defenseBank.q: Defend measuring before optimising a dataframe pipeline.
defenseBank.answer: Memory and time are dominated by one or two columns or steps. `memory_usage(deep=True)` and a timed section show which, and optimising anything else risks complicating code for no measurable gain.

defenseBank.q: A 4 GB CSV must be summarised on a 8 GB laptop. Outline the approach.
defenseBank.answer: Read in chunks and aggregate each chunk into a small result, or convert once to Parquet and read only the needed columns. Either way the peak is a chunk plus the summary, not the file plus a copy.

topics.body: `to_numpy()` drops the index and returns one dtype array, which is what scikit-learn expects. Check the dtype: mixed columns become object.

topics.title: A DataFrame from an array needs names
topics.body: An array has no column names, so the frame supplies them. Without the names, every later selection is positional and fragile.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

arr = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
df = pd.DataFrame(arr, columns=["a", "b"])
print(df.columns.tolist())
print(df["b"].tolist())

topics.title: SQL and Pandas say the same thing
topics.body: SELECT is column selection, WHERE is a mask, GROUP BY is groupby, JOIN is merge. Knowing the mapping is how a query becomes a frame and back.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Pune", "Pune", "Delhi"], "sales": [10, 20, 5]})
out = df[df["sales"] > 5].groupby("city")["sales"].sum()
print(out.to_dict())

topics.title: Split before you compute statistics
topics.body: Fit any statistic on the training rows and apply it to the test rows. Computing the mean over the full table leaks test information into training.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3, 100]})
train = df.iloc[:3]
test = df.iloc[3:]
mean = train["x"].mean()
print(mean, round(float((test["x"] - mean).abs().iloc[0]), 1))

topics.title: Encode categories for a model
topics.body: One-hot encoding is the safe default for a nominal category; an integer code implies an order the model will use.

X = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["city"], dtype=int)
print(X.columns.tolist())
print(X.shape)

interviewBank.q: What is data leakage, in one concrete Pandas example?
interviewBank.answer: Filling missing values or scaling with a statistic computed on the full dataset before splitting. The test rows influenced the transformation, so the validation score is optimistic and does not survive production.

interviewBank.q: Why does scikit-learn prefer a NumPy array while analysis prefers a DataFrame?
interviewBank.answer: The estimator needs a numeric matrix with no labels and no mixed dtypes, so an array is the unambiguous input. Analysis needs names, alignment and mixed types, which the frame provides; `to_numpy` is the boundary.

defenseBank.q: Defend one-hot encoding over integer codes for city.
defenseBank.answer: City is nominal: an integer code tells the model Pune is between Delhi and Mumbai, which is false. One-hot removes the invented order at the cost of more columns, which is manageable for a small vocabulary.
steps: Name the cost of the fix.

defenseBank.q: A pipeline scores 0.98 in validation and 0.6 in production. Give your first hypothesis.
defenseBank.answer: Leakage: a feature or a transformation saw information it will not have in production, usually statistics computed before the split or a column derived from the target. Verify by rebuilding the split first, then the transforms inside it.

interviewBank.q: Walk an interviewer through a Pandas project in four sentences.
interviewBank.answer: The question and the grain, the data and its quality problems, the transformations and why each was chosen, then the finding with its denominator and the check that would falsify it. Four sentences prove you can hold the whole pipeline.

interviewBank.q: How do you answer "what was the hardest bug"?
interviewBank.answer: Name a bug with a cause, not a symptom: a merge that fanned out because the key was not unique, found by comparing row counts, fixed with `validate` and a dedupe. The lesson is the check, not the fix.

defenseBank.q: Defend including a cleaning notebook in your portfolio.
defenseBank.answer: It shows the judgement employers test: what was wrong with the data, which rows were removed and why, and what the numbers looked like before and after. A model with no cleaning trail cannot be audited.

defenseBank.q: Your manager asks for one chart. What do you deliver instead, and why?
defenseBank.answer: The chart plus the table it came from and the two-line finding. The table lets them check the number and reuse it; the finding states what the chart means, which is the part they actually asked for.
